prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B043) at rank 1, but having read all eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks to the head of my configuration. B006 is the only candidate that seven of eight members ranked, with two first places and four top-three placements, and the reasons given are scientific rather than merely popular. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a decisive idea, and Ye's group turned it into a 10^-18 instrument with traceable systematics. As an instrument builder I trust this kind of result: performance is quantified, independently reproduced at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and the downstream physics (tests of relativity at the millimetre scale, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a path to redefining the second) is concrete. The two-name credit is clean and the maturity is not in doubt.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Ulf Danielsson and Olle Eriksson both flag: the 2005 frequency-comb prize and Wineland's 2012 ion-clock prize already cover the foundations of optical metrology, so some will read lattice clocks as an advance in precision rather than a new discovery. There are also real competing claims on the 10^-18 milestone (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, the PTB and NIST groups), and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical consequence is still ahead.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks B006 first as a textbook case of a measurement advance that opens new physics, with a clean Katori-Ye attribution and independent confirmation worldwide.
responses.response: I agree on the science and attribution. Where I would add care is the citation wording: it should credit the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 10^-18, not 'precision' in general, so that the prize is clearly about a new capability and not a refinement of the comb. I share your caution that Lemonde, Ludlow and the Yb and Hg clock groups will be cited against any two-name award, and I would ask for an expert report on who held priority at the 10^-18 level before we finalise.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson ranks IceCube (B043) first as a clear, nature-driven new window on the Universe, and ranks B006 only sixth because it overlaps with the earlier frequency-comb prize and may look incremental.
responses.response: I agree with you on IceCube and I voted the same way, but I do not think the overlap argument holds against B006. The comb prize recognised a ruler for optical frequencies; the lattice clock is a different invention, a way to hold a many-atom ensemble at a magic wavelength so it is free of first-order light shifts. That is a distinct physical idea with its own priority record. On B043 itself, Bernhard Mehlig and Eva Olsson note that the source associations are modest in significance. The diffuse flux is solid but the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane results are still developing, and I now think that argues for waiting a few years for B043, not for dropping it.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson puts topological insulators (B004) first as a genuinely new state of matter with strong theory-to-experiment links, but flags that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not credited.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and it is the main reason I keep B004 as an alternative and not my lead. Kane and Mele supplied the theory, and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment followed the BHZ prediction, so a three-name award either leaves out the HgTe proposers or leaves out the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan. Bernhard Mehlig also raises the 2016 topological-phases prize as an overlap. This is outside my expertise, so I defer to you and Mehlig on whether the Z2 step is distinct enough from 2016 to stand alone.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B009) first and also supports aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B012), while declaring that her own microscopy background could bias her view of B012.
responses.response: I appreciate your openness about B012, which I also ranked second. I think it is a real instrument breakthrough with strong maturity, but you raised the questions that leave me unwilling to lead with it. Only three of us ranked it, Knut Urban is missing from the credited names, and the Chemistry Prize is a plausible home. For B009 I am more cautious than you: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and Olle Eriksson and Ulf Danielsson each call timing possibly early. I would rather revisit it in a few years than reward it now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept lattice clocks as a new invention, given the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, or treat them as incremental.
Priority at the 10^-18 milestone among Katori, Ye, and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, which I know only from memory and which needs an expert report.
Whether a single two-person prize is the best use of the year, or whether a second distinct part could be added without exceeding three laureates.
How robust the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 source associations will look in a few years, which decides whether B043 can be cited for more than the diffuse flux.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, not IceCube, and I have no stated ties to the atomic-clock or other shortlisted groups. My professional proximity to astroparticle detector work is a possible bias towards B043, which I have tried to correct for.
